# Novice Sequencing Experiments: Order of Strength and Speed-Strength Means Mattered Little; Depth Jumps Beat Both

**What it is** — The authors report a set of experiments on novices in speed-strength sports (researchers named as "Purvin, Khodykin, Deniskin, Tatian and Chernousov", names checked against the page image; no dates, sample sizes or statistics are given) (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288):
1. **Order across the preparatory period.** "the sequence of means in the preparatory period (beginning with strength, then speed-strength means, or vice-versa) has no real significance for novices. Consequently, the same effect can be obtained by using these means in any order."
2. **Mixed sessions.** "A relatively larger effect than produced by the above-mentioned variants (with the same volume of training load) occurred in groups who used strength and speed-strength means concurrently by alternating them in mixed training sessions" (the mixed regime used separate sessions "with a rest interval between sessions on the same day", PDF p. 299). The authors add that "the contrasting of stimuli in mixed workouts ... undoubtedly has a positive effect."
3. **Weights then depth jumps.** One novice group did weights in stage 1 and depth jumps in stage 2, a second the reverse, a third both in both stages (not in the same workout). "the first variant was more effective for developing speed-strength." The concurrent group improved in stage 1 but slowed in stage 2 "due to monotonous repetition"; the reversed group improved most after stage 1 but its speed-strength "were lowest at the end of the second stage."
4. **Within one workout.** Strength-then-speed-strength vs the reverse, with pauses "increased slightly to minimise the influence of the positive after-effect", plus a depth-jump group: "There was no statistically significant difference in speed-strength of the subjects in the first two groups. The largest increase in all the parameters of the control movement was discovered in the third group." Depth jumps gave "significantly larger improvement in speed-strength fitness for a smaller volume of training."

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for experiment 4: "any training influence will leave significant traces in an untrained person. The body is unable to react selectively to a chiefly strength or speed-strength means in one workout. In addition, the period over which the traces of the training stimulus are maintained is apparently longer than the duration of the after-effect of prior tonic work. Within one workout, the traces of all the training tasks are summed" (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288). For experiment 3, the reversed group's early gain is put down to "the larger training effect of the plyometric method." No mechanism is given for the "monotonous repetition" slowdown.

**When to apply** — With novices, do not spend planning effort on whether strength or speed-strength work comes first in a session; the authors found no significant difference. Across stages, their data favour heavy resistance first and depth jumps after. The authors limit the within-workout finding to novices: "it is very likely that their lower level of special fitness excluded the possibility for exploiting this phenomenon adequately. A well-trained athlete can expect the preceding strength work to have a positive effect ... However, the validity of this hypothesis can be established conclusively only by careful experimentation" (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288). Eric's baseline: "Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 173, Inferred). Inference: the weights-then-depth-jumps result fits that order for a first-year athlete, though the authors tested speed-strength, not skill.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The authors' own summary on the next page reads: "A slightly smaller effect is obtained by the concurrent use of strength and speed-strength means in one training session or their sequential use in successive sessions" and "Least effective is the sequence of strength followed by speed-strength means during the same session" (PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289). The second sentence ranks strength-then-speed-strength in one session last, while PDF p. 299 found "no statistically significant difference" between that order and its reverse. The PDF p. 299 statement that order "has no real significance for novices" also sits uneasily with experiment 3 on the same page, where weights-then-depth-jumps beat the reverse order in novices. The book also states, in 5.2.4, that resistance plus plyometrics works best "provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277), which sits against experiment 4's null within-session result in novices. Inference: the first summary sentence, that mixed or successive-session use gives "A slightly smaller effect", compares them with the best variant (the Fig 5.13 complexes), while PDF p. 299 compares mixed sessions with the two order variants, so those two statements do not conflict. These results do not support claims about trained athletes; the authors say so. Their hypothesis that trained athletes benefit from a strength after-effect is untested in this text. Issurin, also in this library, sequences by fatigue tolerance: explosive strength needs a well-rested to slightly fatigued athlete ([[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]]), which is a different rule from either order tested here.

**Example** — The authors' third experiment: novices doing weights in stage 1 and depth jumps in stage 2 developed speed-strength best; the reverse order gained fastest at first but ended lowest (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288).

**Related** — [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]] (the conclusions the authors draw), [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the after-effect within a session), [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]], [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]], [[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]] (5.2.4, the resistance-before-plyometrics rule)

=================== claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique.md
# Too Much Heavy Strength Work Lowers Speed, Explosiveness and Technique; Speed-Strength Gains Stop After About 12-18 Weeks

**What it is** — The authors grant that general heavy resistance exercises "enable the athlete to reach the necessary level of absolute strength, to provide general physical conditioning and to train the neuromuscular system non-specifically," but "it is undesirable to use them extensively during specialised training phases, since they can diminish speed and explosiveness. High volume strength loads used after a phase of specialised jump training can substantially reduce the existing level of explosive strength (by as much as 30%)" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291; all figures in this entry checked against the page image). Supporting reports, all cited without dates except Deniskin: Kotz, "prolonged, heavy workloads slow the contraction speed of trained muscles"; Filinov, "excessively heavy strength loads diminish the force and speed of boxers' punches"; Deniskin (1976), "prolonged use of high volume strength loads diminishes the power and speed of weightlifters, high jumpers and triple jumpers." On dose: "speed-strength and strength-speed cease to increase after a certain volume of heavy strength training has been executed. Deniskin observed this phenomenon after 18 weeks (54 workouts) of strength training. Other studies have also noted the same phenomenon after 50-60 training sessions or approximately 12 weeks of training." On technique, Siff writes (the passage names Verkhoshansky in the third person): "research by Verkhoshansky and colleagues has established that excessive maximum strength training can impair speed-strength and technical skill in boxers (Verkhoshansky, 1977). It can also lead to a deterioration of several months' duration in the technique of weightlifters and javelin throwers" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291).

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the technique loss: "The negative influence of heavy strength training on sports technique may be due substantially to deterioration of the speed-strength qualities of the neuromuscular system," and "heavy training loads reduce one's ability to control movements, primarily of their most complex technical phases" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). For the plateau they give a dose argument only: "there are certain volumes and durations of strength training that are essential for achieving an optimum training effect. # Aerobic vs Anaerobic Circuits: Rough Guidelines for Reps, Load, Rest and Laps

**What it is** — The authors give "rough guidelines," warning that "a considerable degree of individuality is involved and no precise figures can be quoted to be universally appropriate for everyone" (PDF p. 315 / printed p. 304, checked against the page image). Cardiovascular circuits "all fall under the category of CCT," and "A true aerobic circuit would involve the predominant use of very low resistance devices or prolonged rhythmic movements"; anaerobic circuits "may be either CCT (continuous) or ICT (interval), with the former resulting largely in muscle endurance, and variations of the latter developing strength, power, muscle endurance, speed or flexibility."

| | Cardiovascular (aerobic) circuits | Anaerobic circuits |
|---|---|---|
| Rest | "Continuous activity or very brief intervals" between stations | "Rest intervals between stations to permit some recovery (1-4 minutes)" |
| Station mix | aerobic activity alternating "between resistance stations" | "Fewer aerobic stations and more resistance stations" |
| Reps per resistance station | "20-40" | "3-8" |
| Load | "usually not more than 30% of 1RM" | "usually more than 70% of 1RM" |
| Laps ("excursions") | "5-10" | "3-5" |

# Circuit Layout Variants: A Two-Station Circuit Is a Superset, and Circuits Can Backtrack, Stagger, Detour, Pyramid or Strip

**What it is** — The authors propose "a systems approach adapted from applied mathematics" to circuits. "The traditional approach requires one to proceed from starting station to terminal station for a certain number of sets, without backtracking, omitting stations or diverting to extra equipment"; "The more generalised approach includes the possibility of backtracking, omitting stations, altering the sequence of stations, diverting to other equipment, using different speeds of movement or time periods on each station, changing the exercise pattern at each station, and changing the types of muscle contraction at each station" (PDF p. 320 / printed p. 309, checked against the page image). The variants, each shown in a figure checked against the page images (PDF pp. 320-322 / printed pp. 309-311):
- **Superset = two-station circuit.** "a circuit with two stations is exactly the same as a superset with two exercises (Fig 5.29)."
- **Retrophase circuit.** "backtrack by one station for every two stations completed" (Fig 5.30); backtracking more "may cause confusion if there is a large group."
- **Dual-set retrophase and sequenced supersets.** "complete two sets at each station before moving to the next station, then backtrack to complete the remaining two sets" (Fig 5.31b); or superset A and B "before going on to superset exercises C and D" (Fig 5.31a).
- **Staggered or zig-zag circuit.** Lets clients "progress through portions of a circuit easily without obstructing others"; some do the inner circuit, some the outer, advanced clients "zigzag through the entire circuit," with aerobic stations in the middle of the floor (Fig 5.32).
- **Detour circuit.** Clients "exit at a particular point to perform a sub-circuit" of free weights, aerobic, skill, flexibility, running, plyometric or water exercises elsewhere (Fig 5.33).
- **Other variants** (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311): repetitions to failure at each station; "pyramid circuits" in which load rises "from 40-80% of 1RM" and reps fall "e.g. from 10 to 4" with each lap; "stripping circuits" that pyramid up to "a 6RM or 10RM on each station, then progressively strip the load down," generally "about 10kg each time"; and variable-repetition or variable-interval sets. Aqualand circuits mix land and water stations (Figs 5.21-5.23, PDF pp. 317-318).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated purposes: more variety "thereby diminishing the likelihood of stagnation and boredom" (PDF p. 320 / printed p. 309), less crowding at stations (staggered circuits), and access to equipment outside the circuit (detours). For water stations they give a physical reason: "the resistance offered by water increases with the velocity of movement (actually, the square of the velocity)" and "is also directly proportional to the area of the limb pushing against the water" (PDF p. 317 / printed p. 306, checked against the page image).

**When to apply** — Running a large group through limited equipment, or adding variety to a circuit block without changing its exercises. Inference: the superset equivalence is useful when writing programmes: a two-exercise superset can be planned and progressed with the same rules as a circuit. Inference: a staggered layout suits a team lift where position groups share racks, since an inner and outer loop keep groups from queuing.

**When NOT to apply** — The variants are design options, not tested training methods, hence `untested`. Retrophase and staggered layouts add complexity; the authors themselves warn that backtracking "may cause confusion" with large groups. Stripping and failure-based circuits raise fatigue; the authors say working to failure "makes it highly advisable that you have a 'spotting' partner nearby" (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311). For aqualand circuits they note it is "inadvisable to have water dripping from wet athletes on the floor and onto indoor apparatus" and that pool water must be changed regularly (PDF pp. 317-318).

**Example** — The authors' own stripping set: pyramid "from 10 repetitions with 60kg up to 6 repetitions with 100kg," then the partner strips the bar to 90 kg, 80 kg and 70 kg, with sets to failure at each load (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311, checked against the page image).

**Related** — [[framework--continuous-interval-and-mixed-circuit-training-classification]], [[heuristic--setchinov-alternation-for-circuit-station-sequencing]], [[heuristic--circuit-progression-load-prescription-and-novice-pre-testing]], [[heuristic--parachute-resistance-sizing-progression-and-contrast-release]] (the same velocity-squared drag relation, for parachutes), [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]

- **Superset = two-station circuit.** "a circuit with two stations is exactly the same as a superset with two exercises (Fig 5.29)."
- **Retrophase circuit.** "backtrack by one station for every two stations completed" (Fig 5.30); backtracking more "may cause confusion if there is a large group."
- **Dual-set retrophase and sequenced supersets.** "complete two sets at each station before moving to the next station, then backtrack to complete the remaining two sets" (Fig 5.31b); or superset A and B "before going on to superset exercises C and D" (Fig 5.31a).
- **Staggered or zig-zag circuit.** Lets clients "progress through portions of a circuit easily without obstructing others"; some do the inner circuit, some the outer, advanced clients "zigzag through the entire circuit," with aerobic stations in the middle of the floor (Fig 5.32).
- **Detour circuit.** Clients "exit at a particular point to perform a sub-circuit" of free weights, aerobic, skill, flexibility, running, plyometric or water exercises elsewhere (Fig 5.33).
- **Other variants** (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311): repetitions to failure at each station; "pyramid circuits" in which load rises "from 40-80% of 1RM" and reps fall "e.g. from 10 to 4" with each lap; "stripping circuits" that pyramid up to "a 6RM or 10RM on each station, then progressively strip the load down," generally "about 10kg each time"; and variable-repetition or variable-interval sets. Aqualand circuits mix land and water stations (Figs 5.21-5.23, PDF pp. 317-318).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated purposes: more variety "thereby diminishing the likelihood of stagnation and boredom" (PDF p. 320 / printed p. 309), less crowding at stations (staggered circuits), and access to equipment outside the circuit (detours). For water stations they give a physical reason: "the resistance offered by water increases with the velocity of movement (actually, the square of the velocity)" and "is also directly proportional to the area of the limb pushing against the water" (PDF p. 317 / printed p. 306, checked against the page image).

**When to apply** — Running a large group through limited equipment, or adding variety to a circuit block without changing its exercises. Inference: the superset equivalence is useful when writing programmes: a two-exercise superset can be planned and progressed with the same rules as a circuit. Inference: a staggered layout suits a team lift where position groups share racks, since an inner and outer loop keep groups from queuing.

**When NOT to apply** — The variants are design options, not tested training methods, hence `untested`. Retrophase and staggered layouts add complexity; the authors themselves warn that backtracking "may cause confusion" with large groups. Stripping and failure-based circuits raise fatigue; the authors say working to failure "makes it highly advisable that you have a 'spotting' partner nearby" (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311). For aqualand circuits they note it is "inadvisable to have water dripping from wet athletes on the floor and onto indoor apparatus" and that pool water must be changed regularly (PDF pp. 317-318).

**Example** — The authors' own stripping set: pyramid "from 10 repetitions with 60kg up to 6 repetitions with 100kg," then the partner strips the bar to 90 kg, 80 kg and 70 kg, with sets to failure at each load (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311, checked against the page image).

# After a Concentrated Block, Unload and Wait: Gains Commonly Appear After a 1-3 Week Latency

**What it is** — The authors warn: "The system is not without its dangers, since concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength. After a phase of emphasis on heavy strength training, there may be an increase in muscle stiffness and a loss of explosive strength, sporting skill or speed." Their rule, italicised in the original: "a diminished loading and restorative period has to be observed after a given concentrated loading phase to allow the body to supercompensate to the desired level of preparedness." The timing: "The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without adequate restoration. Not only does premature imposition of concentrated loading suppress the delayed training effect of the previous stage, but it also lowers the effectiveness of future training" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the conjugate sequence system is based on exploitation of the delayed training effect" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), so the next block must start once that effect has appeared, not before. No physiological mechanism is given in this section. Inference: the authors frame the restorative period as supercompensation; the two-factor (fitness-fatigue) reading in this library would describe the same pattern as fatigue clearing to reveal fitness, and the book does not choose between them here.

**When to apply** — After any 4-8 week block that concentrates on one quality, plan a lower-load period before the next concentrated block. Inference: judge the block's result after the 1-3 week latency, not on the last day of loading. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred). Inference: the 1-3 week latency is a reason to leave slack between blocks in that roadmap, so a delayed gain is not cut short by the next block.

**When NOT to apply** — The 1-3 week figure is "most commonly," with no study named. It is a latency to the onset of gains. Chapter 6 gives a different number for a different quantity: the long-term delayed training effect "was observed to last from 4-12 weeks during the long-term stages of strength preparation," its duration "approximately equal to the duration of the strength training stage," and its appearance "individualised" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image). **Contested across the library:** Bompa & Haff (5th ed.), not Supertraining, write that "Siff and Verkhoshansky (83) suggested that performance gains may occur 4 to 12 weeks after the cessation of the concentrated loading phase" (Bompa & Haff 5e, PDF idx 61 of the Drive copy), and the Bompa entry [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] repeats this as a 4-12 week delay. That matches neither Supertraining statement: 5.3.3 gives a 1-3 week latency to gains (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294); Chapter 6 gives 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364). Fig 6.31 on that page (checked against the page image) shows the timing: the trained qualities (F1-F3) are depressed during the concentrated loading stage T1 and climb during T2, which begins where T1 ends (dashed line). The other 4-12 week figures in the book are also durations: Chapter 6 calls unidirectional training "for prolonged stages (4-12 weeks)" very effective (PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370, text layer), and the Addendum says "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks," with the delayed effect's duration "equal to the duration of the stage" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, text layer). Use the onset figure for when to expect a result and the duration figure for how long it may hold. Chapter 6 also qualifies the warning: during the emergence of the delayed effect "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364), so the restorative period is about volume, not a full stop.

**Example** — The authors' own: after a 4-8 week concentrated strength block, the gains "may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Inference: an off-season strength block ending in late March would be judged in April, and the speed-emphasis block that follows would open at lower volume rather than at full load.

**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the delayed training effect), [[case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means]] (rest weeks between stages), [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]] (4.1.1, speed-strength up 18-25% after a 10-day rest, PDF p. 213; an in-library case for a short latency), [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]

# Across Stages: Jumps, Then Barbell Work, Then Depth Jumps; Staying on One Means Stalls or Reverses Progress

**What it is** — Three "equivalent groups of jumpers of average qualification" trained "Under natural training conditions" (Verkhoshansky & Aganin 1970; Fig 5.13, verified against the page image; PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289). All used special jumping exercises in stage 1. Group 1 stayed on jumps for all three stages. Group 2 switched to barbell exercises in stage 2 and stayed there. Group 3 switched to barbell exercises in stage 2 and to depth jumps in stage 3. "The special strength training indicators displayed a clear tendency to stabilise in groups 1 and 2 after the first and second stages respectively, and in group 1, even to decrease during the third stage." The figure shows group 3's line rising through all three stages, group 2's flat in stage 3, and group 1's flattening in stage 2 and dipping in stage 3. The authors conclude: "the sequential use of means with higher, specific training effects clearly produces a positive result. At the same time, the use of the same means, even with an increase in volume, not only does not produce a positive change, but decreases the existing level of special strength fitness." From this and the novice work they draw two rules "for the sequential use of training means over a given period" (PDF pp. 300-301 / printed pp. 289-290):
- "Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training"
- "Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises, but not before."

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the sequential-means logic of 5.3: each means loses effect as the body adapts, so a stronger means must follow (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287). Fig 5.13 shows only the direction of the control indicators; it has no numerical axis. No physiological mechanism is given for why depth jumps must follow, not precede, strength work. Inference: the Deniskin (1976) laboratory study on the next page (heavy resistance, then two depth-jump stages) is the authors' supporting case for the second rule; see Related.

**When to apply** — Ordering the means for jumpers or other speed-strength athletes over an off-season: general jumping first, barbell strength next, intense depth jumps last. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred). Inference: the authors' order also runs from lower to higher training effect, which fits that rule; for a football off-season this would read as general jumps and med-ball work, then a barbell-strength block, then depth jumps closer to the period where speed-strength is needed.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The same summary list ranks variants differently from the experiments reported a page earlier: it calls strength followed by speed-strength in the same session "Least effective" (PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289), while PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288 found "no statistically significant difference" between that order and its reverse in novices (see [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]]); and the first rule, "Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training" (PDF p. 301), sits against the novice finding that this order "has no real significance for novices" (PDF p. 299) and against 5.2.4's statement that resistance work should precede plyometrics "in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277). The rules come from novices and "athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 300); the authors say so in the lead-in to the list. No group sizes, statistics or units are given for Fig 5.13. Inference: the first rule reads as order over a period (stages), not within one session, since the authors introduce the rules as "for the sequential use of training means over a given period," though the same list mixes session-level and stage-level rankings; it should not be read as "lift after you jump" in a single workout, which is a separate question. Issurin 2016 questions the evidence for Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional sequencing in team and combat sports (see [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: group 3 (jumps, then barbell, then depth jumps) kept improving through stage 3, while group 1 (jumps throughout) levelled off and then declined (Fig 5.13, PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289).

**Related** — [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]], [[case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]] (Fig 5.18 gives the same order with "jumps with weights" added), [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]], [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]], [[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]] (5.2.4, resistance before plyometrics in a session)

# Accelerating Specific Adaptation: Model the Sport, Sequence Its Demands, and Plan for Delays

**What it is** — "The principle of accelerating specific adaptation emphasizes the key role of special strength training as the foundation for developing sports proficiency ... The idea is that specific adaptation should be accelerated by advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected to be produced by the current training regime." In practice, "the task of functional specialisation should be based on accurate modelling of all aspects of the motor activity," whose requirements "are then presented to the body in a specific sequence during the STP (Sports Training Process) in order to accelerate adaptation" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296, checked against the page image). The authors list four means of achieving it: "controlling the post-training supercompensatory phases by using the conjugate sequence method of training, by the heterochronicity principle of superimposed cycles of training the different components of fitness, by converging the partial effects of the training means, or by correctly periodised full or partial restoration after training (see 8.5)." It also "necessitates using statistical data which reflect the basic trends in the dynamics of the athlete's specific motor abilities in the given sport (see 2.2.3)" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296).

**Why it works** — The authors' claim of effect: "Specialised means of strength training selected to take into account the specific movements of the given sport and the participant's existing level of fitness produce a timely and substantial increase in relative and starting strength, significantly exceeding the average indices typical of the training of that type of athlete," and "the use of complex, novel means of strength training enable highly qualified athletes to avoid the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). No data or study is given for either statement on this page.

**When to apply** — Long-range planning for an athlete with a target date: model the sport's demands, sequence them, track the athlete's abilities against norms for the sport, and keep a backup plan. The authors' contingency rule is the most directly usable part: success "depends on anticipating any conditions which may delay the subsequent course of the STP," and when fitness lags "due to unforeseen circumstances such as adaptational idiosyncrasies, illness or injury ... a contingency plan should always be available to maintain the fitness level of those systems which can still be exercised" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Eric's baseline: "Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 129, Explicit). Inference: the contingency rule (train what can still be trained during injury) is the authors' version of keeping the uninjured systems loaded during RTP.

**When NOT to apply** — **Two definitions in the book.** In 5.3.3 the same term names a volume saving: "the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration of specific adaptation (see 5.4.2)" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Section 5.4.2, which that sentence points to, defines it as "advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected" and does not mention the 20% figure (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Inference: the two can coexist (reach the peak sooner with less volume), but the book never says so; quote whichever definition is meant. The effect claims are given without data. The "statistical data" on ability trends that the principle requires (2.2.3) may not exist for a given sport or population.

**Example** — The authors' own: highly qualified athletes using "complex, novel means of strength training" to avoid "the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Inference: an injured lineman who cannot squat keeps upper-body and single-leg work going under the contingency rule, so the systems that can still be trained do not detrain.

**Related** — [[framework--four-principles-of-special-strength-training-organisation]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]] (the 20% definition), [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[principle--converging-partial-effects-of-strength-training-means]], [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]

=================== principle--sequentially-introduce-means-of-greater-training-effect.md
# Introduce Means of Gradually Greater Training Effect, Matched to the Athlete's Current Special Fitness

**What it is** — In 5.3.2, "A Sequential System of Training Means," the authors argue that the development of a specific motor ability "occurs in a specific pattern," so "it is necessary to sequentially improve the functioning of those systems and physiological mechanisms which are crucial for developing a specific motor ability" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). "Progressive functional changes in some systems act as prerequisites for improving the performance of other systems." The rule: "the means used should elicit a definite training effect, but its magnitude should correspond to the body's current level of specific fitness and increase in conjunction with the latter." Hence "the necessity ... for devising a scheme for sequentially introducing means of gradually greater training effect into training." The new means "should be novel, so as to promote a greater training effect by compelling the adaptive processes to transcend any performance plateau" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason is that earlier functional changes are prerequisites for later ones, and that "Specificity becomes more relevant to one's state of fitness as sports proficiency increases. At the same time, the role of the means used to develop trainability grows" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Novelty is given as the way past a plateau; no physiological mechanism is named. Inference: this is the same logic as the first 4.1.2 generalization (the training effect of any means diminishes as special physical fitness increases; see the taxonomy entry in Related).

**When to apply** — When selecting means for a block, check that each one is strong enough for the athlete's current level and no stronger than needed, and plan the next, stronger means before the current one stops working. The authors name two common errors to avoid: means "selected on the spur of the moment without considering their precise training effect and often on the basis of what is currently fashionable or subjectively preferred," and "means which are highly effective during more advanced stages of training ... used inappropriately during the early stages of the yearly cycle or in the beginning stages of multi-year training." They also criticise a repertoire that "is usually extremely limited and is repeated in much the same way from year to year" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred). Inference: the authors' "gradually greater training effect" is a second axis on that spectrum: within a category, means can be ranked by strength of effect.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors note a limit of the evidence: "Research has investigated changing the special training means only once or twice during the period of study," while practical use needs "multiple changes" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292), so multi-change sequences are argued, not tested, here. The principle needs a ranking of means by training effect, which the authors say requires "experimental assessment of the training effect and categorisation of the specific complex of means" (PDF p. 308 / printed p. 297); without it the ranking is a guess. "Novel" means are not the same as random variety: the authors elsewhere call random combination less effective (see Related).

**Example** — The authors' own error case: highly effective advanced means (their example category, not a named exercise) used at the start of a yearly cycle or of a young athlete's career (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Inference: depth jumps from high boxes in a freshman's first summer would be that error; the 5.3 jumper study placed them in the third stage.

**Related** — [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the five generalizations), [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]], [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]] (5.4.4, the same principle applied), [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]

Inference: the Deniskin (1976) laboratory study on the next page (heavy resistance, then two depth-jump stages) is the authors' supporting case for the second rule; see Related.

**When to apply** — Ordering the means for jumpers or other speed-strength athletes over an off-season: general jumping first, barbell strength next, intense depth jumps last. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred). Inference: the authors' order also runs from lower to higher training effect, which fits that rule; for a football off-season this would read as general jumps and med-ball work, then a barbell-strength block, then depth jumps closer to the period where speed-strength is needed.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The same summary list ranks variants differently from the experiments reported a page earlier: it calls strength followed by speed-strength in the same session "Least effective" (PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289), while PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288 found "no statistically significant difference" between that order and its reverse in novices (see [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]]); and the first rule, "Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training" (PDF p. 301), sits against the novice finding that this order "has no real significance for novices" (PDF p. 299) and against 5.2.4's statement that resistance work should precede plyometrics "in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277). The rules come from novices and "athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 300); the authors say so in the lead-in to the list. No group sizes, statistics or units are given for Fig 5.13. Inference: the first rule reads as order over a period (stages), not within one session, since the authors introduce the rules as "for the sequential use of training means over a given period," though the same list mixes session-level and stage-level rankings; it should not be read as "lift after you jump" in a single workout, which is a separate question. Issurin 2016 questions the evidence for Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional sequencing in team and combat sports (see [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]).

=================== principle--accelerating-specific-adaptation.md
# Accelerating Specific Adaptation: Model the Sport, Sequence Its Demands, and Plan for Delays

**What it is** — "The principle of accelerating specific adaptation emphasizes the key role of special strength training as the foundation for developing sports proficiency ... The idea is that specific adaptation should be accelerated by advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected to be produced by the current training regime." In practice, "the task of functional specialisation should be based on accurate modelling of all aspects of the motor activity," whose requirements "are then presented to the body in a specific sequence during the STP (Sports Training Process) in order to accelerate adaptation" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296, checked against the page image). The authors list four means of achieving it: "controlling the post-training supercompensatory phases by using the conjugate sequence method of training, by the heterochronicity principle of superimposed cycles of training the different components of fitness, by converging the partial effects of the training means, or by correctly periodised full or partial restoration after training (see 8.5)." It also "necessitates using statistical data which reflect the basic trends in the dynamics of the athlete's specific motor abilities in the given sport (see 2.2.3)" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296).

**Why it works** — The authors' claim of effect: "Specialised means of strength training selected to take into account the specific movements of the given sport and the participant's existing level of fitness produce a timely and substantial increase in relative and starting strength, significantly exceeding the average indices typical of the training of that type of athlete," and "the use of complex, novel means of strength training enable highly qualified athletes to avoid the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). No data or study is given for either statement on this page.

**When to apply** — Long-range planning for an athlete with a target date: model the sport's demands, sequence them, track the athlete's abilities against norms for the sport, and keep a backup plan. The authors' contingency rule is the most directly usable part: success "depends on anticipating any conditions which may delay the subsequent course of the STP," and when fitness lags "due to unforeseen circumstances such as adaptational idiosyncrasies, illness or injury ... a contingency plan should always be available to maintain the fitness level of those systems which can still be exercised" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Eric's baseline: "Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 129, Explicit). Inference: the contingency rule (train what can still be trained during injury) is the authors' version of keeping the uninjured systems loaded during RTP.

**When NOT to apply** — **Two definitions in the book.** In 5.3.3 the same term names a volume saving: "the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration of specific adaptation (see 5.4.2)" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Section 5.4.2, which that sentence points to, defines it as "advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected" and does not mention the 20% figure (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Inference: the two can coexist (reach the peak sooner with less volume), but the book never says so; quote whichever definition is meant. The effect claims are given without data. The "statistical data" on ability trends that the principle requires (2.2.3) may not exist for a given sport or population.

**Example** — The authors' own: highly qualified athletes using "complex, novel means of strength training" to avoid "the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Inference: an injured lineman who cannot squat keeps upper-body and single-leg work going under the contingency rule, so the systems that can still be trained do not detrain.

**Related** — [[framework--four-principles-of-special-strength-training-organisation]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]] (the 20% definition), [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[principle--converging-partial-effects-of-strength-training-means]], [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]

=================== principle--sequentially-introduce-means-of-greater-training-effect.md
# Introduce Means of Gradually Greater Training Effect, Matched to the Athlete's Current Special Fitness

**What it is** — In 5.3.2, "A Sequential System of Training Means," the authors argue that the development of a specific motor ability "occurs in a specific pattern," so "it is necessary to sequentially improve the functioning of those systems and physiological mechanisms which are crucial for developing a specific motor ability" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). "Progressive functional changes in some systems act as prerequisites for improving the performance of other systems." The rule: "the means used should elicit a definite training effect, but its magnitude should correspond to the body's current level of specific fitness and increase in conjunction with the latter." Hence "the necessity ... for devising a scheme for sequentially introducing means of gradually greater training effect into training." The new means "should be novel, so as to promote a greater training effect by compelling the adaptive processes to transcend any performance plateau" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason is that earlier functional changes are prerequisites for later ones, and that "Specificity becomes more relevant to one's state of fitness as sports proficiency increases. At the same time, the role of the means used to develop trainability grows" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Novelty is given as the way past a plateau; no physiological mechanism is named. Inference: this is the same logic as the first 4.1.2 generalization (the training effect of any means diminishes as special physical fitness increases; see the taxonomy entry in Related).

**When to apply** — When selecting means for a block, check that each one is strong enough for the athlete's current level and no stronger than needed, and plan the next, stronger means before the current one stops working. The authors name two common errors to avoid: means "selected on the spur of the moment without considering their precise training effect and often on the basis of what is currently fashionable or subjectively preferred," and "means which are highly effective during more advanced stages of training ... used inappropriately during the early stages of the yearly cycle or in the beginning stages of multi-year training." They also criticise a repertoire that "is usually extremely limited and is repeated in much the same way from year to year" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred). Inference: the authors' "gradually greater training effect" is a second axis on that spectrum: within a category, means can be ranked by strength of effect.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors note a limit of the evidence: "Research has investigated changing the special training means only once or twice during the period of study," while practical use needs "multiple changes" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292), so multi-change sequences are argued, not tested, here. The principle needs a ranking of means by training effect, which the authors say requires "experimental assessment of the training effect and categorisation of the specific complex of means" (PDF p. 308 / printed p. 297); without it the ranking is a guess. "Novel" means are not the same as random variety: the authors elsewhere call random combination less effective (see Related).

**Example** — The authors' own error case: highly effective advanced means (their example category, not a named exercise) used at the start of a yearly cycle or of a young athlete's career (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Inference: depth jumps from high boxes in a freshman's first summer would be that error; the 5.3 jumper study placed them in the third stage.

**Related** — [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the five generalizations), [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]], [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]] (5.4.4, the same principle applied), [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]

content.content:
=================== framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading.md
confidence: contested
**What it is** — The authors set out the working conditions for the concentrated phases of the conjugate sequence system (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294, checked against the page image):
1. **Scale and duration.** "Unidirectional emphasis on qualities such as strength or endurance may be used not only in individual workouts but also during each microcycle (Kudelin, 1980; Budokho et al, 1978; Mironenko, 1980). Research has shown that unidirectional training over periods as long as 4-12 weeks can be very effective, especially if the intensity is gradually increased for each form of loading in the given cycle."
2. **Diversity within one emphasis.** "unidirectional loading is effective only if one uses a diverse complex of means with a single primary emphasis, together with a variety of training methods (Fedorova et al, 1975; Platonov & Monograov, 1977; Verkhoshansky, 1977)."
3. **Low intensity of the means.** "an important condition for implementing concentrated loading is the relatively low intensity of the means, since the frequent use of these means already intensifies the training."
4. **Definition.** "the loading may be considered concentrated if its volume in the month in which it is applied constitutes 23-25% of the general volume for the year."
5. **Payoff claimed.** "the effectiveness of the conjugate sequence system with advanced athletes is such that the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration of specific adaptation (see 5.4.2)."

**Why it works** — The authors' one stated reason is condition 3: concentration "already intensifies the training," so intense means on top of it would overload. Chapter 6 repeats this in the same words ("Concentration of unidirectional loading already intensifies the training process, and one should not intensify it further with high intensity means"; PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image). No reason is given for the 23-25% threshold beyond the definition itself, and no source is named for the 20% volume saving.

**When to apply** — Planning a concentrated block for an advanced athlete: fill it with several different exercises that share one emphasis, keep each one moderate in intensity, and expect the month's volume to be about a quarter of the year's. Eric's baseline: "Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 184, Inferred). Inference: a 4-12 week unidirectional block runs past those windows for the qualities it does not train, so the baseline's retention dose would still be needed alongside it; the authors do not address retention of other qualities here.
**When NOT to apply** — The authors warn on the same page that "concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength" (see [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]]). The 23-25% figure is a definition, not a target derived from data. The "acceleration of specific adaptation" is defined here as a volume saving of up to 20%, but 5.4.2 defines it differently, as "advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected to be produced by the current training regime" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296); keep both meanings in view. **Contested by Issurin** for team and combat sports (see [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]). Issurin's own block model also concentrates workloads but on a minimal number of targets per block, not a single one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]).

**Example** — Inference: a 4-week concentrated strength block in which squats, pulls, presses and loaded jumps all serve the strength emphasis, each at moderate loads, with that month carrying close to a quarter of the year's strength volume. The authors give the rule, not a worked plan.
=================== heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades.md
confidence: supported
**What it is** — "Preservation of the training effect means that the load should always produce a training effect by the systematic, timely introduction of more effective training means based on logical continuity," to avoid "the states of stagnation and deterioration described in Chapter 1 (see Fig 1.32)." In practice, "as the training effect of some means decreases, so more effective, newer means are introduced which, in turn, are replaced by even more effective means." This needs "experimental assessment of the training effect and categorisation of the specific complex of means" (PDF p. 308 / printed p. 297). Fig 5.18 (verified against the page image) gives the authors' example for "developing explosive leg strength in the preparation period of a jumper" (Verkhoshansky 1969, 1970): jumping exercises, then barbell exercises, then jumps with weights, then depth jumping, each curve rising and flattening, with a dashed line marking each switch to the next, stronger means. Over years, "The long term use of the conjugate sequence method involves implementing a repetitive, cyclical system of sequentially applied means, each of increasing intensity," revising the complex by "successively replacing those which played an earlier progressive role ... (means A and B) with newer, more effective means (C and D), and finally with still other means (E)" (PDF p. 308 / printed p. 297). Fig 5.19 (verified against the page image, PDF p. 309 / printed p. 298; based on Verkhoshansky 1977) shows year 1 as A, B, C; year 2 as B, C, D; year 3 as C, D, E, each year starting from a higher training-effect level.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the sequential-means premise: "the training effect of any means diminishes as the body adapts to its influence" (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287). They add, for qualified athletes, that "the long-term use of the same means, even if the volume is increased, not only will not increase one's level of special fitness but will also decrease the existing level of speed-strength and especially, maximum strength" (PDF p. 304 / printed p. 293). No physiological mechanism is given.

**When to apply** — Plan the next means before the current one plateaus; each year, drop the weakest means from the bottom of the sequence and add a stronger one at the top. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit, shared team material). Inference: the authors' rule works on a different variable: Prilepin's chart sets the dose within a means, while this heuristic says when to change the means themselves.
**When NOT to apply** — Figs 5.18 and 5.19 are schematics without units or data, so they do not say how long each means lasts. The authors make the method depend on "experimental assessment of the training effect" (PDF p. 308 / printed p. 297); without some measure of when a means has stopped working, the switch points are guesses. The sequence is for a jumper's explosive leg strength in the preparation period; the order for other qualities or sports is not given here. The plan assumes the athlete is still improving; the authors do not address maintenance-only periods such as an in-season phase.

**Example** — The authors' own: a jumper's preparation period moving from jumping exercises to barbell exercises to jumps with weights to depth jumping, switching each time the previous means' curve flattens (Fig 5.18, PDF p. 308 / printed p. 297).
=================== heuristic--setchinov-alternation-for-circuit-station-sequencing.md
confidence: supported
**What it is** — "The effectiveness of any circuit may be enhanced by taking cognizance of the Setchinov phenomenon, which encourages restoration by means of diverting activity performed between exercises. For example, this may entail exercise of upper body muscles alternating with exercise of unfatigued muscles of the legs. In applying this principle to circuit training, upper body stations should then alternately exercise upper and lower body muscles, back and front muscles, or agonistic and antagonistic muscles" (PDF p. 319 / printed p. 308, checked against the page image). The authors' layouts (Figs 5.25-5.28, verified against the page image, PDF p. 319 / printed p. 308; described in the text on PDF pp. 319-320): aerobic stations (AS) alternating one-for-one with resistance stations (RS) that alternate upper and lower body (Fig 5.25); one aerobic station followed by two resistance stations, "again alternately exercising the upper and lower (or front/back, left/right, etc.) parts of the body" (Fig 5.27); and one aerobic station followed by three resistance stations (Fig 5.28). Circuits aimed "more on muscle endurance or strength, can begin with an aerobics station, then progress through a succession of resistance stations, also preferably sequenced in accordance with the Setchinov principle."

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the one in the name: diverting activity between exercises "encourages restoration" of the muscles just worked (PDF p. 319 / printed p. 308). They do not explain how. Inference: the Setchinov (Sechenov) active-rest effect is a classical observation that working other muscles during a rest period speeds recovery of the fatigued ones; the book cites no study for it here, and its size in modern studies is not checked in this entry.

**When to apply** — Ordering any circuit so that consecutive stations load different regions, which lets the athlete keep moving while each region recovers. Inference: the same rule can pair exercises in a superset within a strength session. Inference: in a football off-season circuit, a lower-body station (split squat) followed by an upper pull (row), then a lower-body hinge, then an upper push, follows the authors' rule.
**When NOT to apply** — Alternation helps local recovery, not whole-body fatigue: a circuit that alternates regions but has no rest still limits load and speed, which is the authors' main criticism of traditional circuits (see Related). For maximal strength or power work the authors want rest intervals, not just alternation (PDF p. 315 / printed p. 304). The authors give no data for how much the Setchinov effect improves a circuit.

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 5.25, aerobic stations such as fixed cycles or skipping alternating with resistance stations, "with the latter alternating between upper and lower body movements" (PDF p. 319 / printed p. 308).
=================== heuristic--circuit-progression-load-prescription-and-novice-pre-testing.md
confidence: supported
**What it is** — "there is no such entity as the best circuit, only the most appropriate and effective circuit for achieving specific fitness aims in a particular person at a particular stage of training." Each circuit should be run at beginner, intermediate and advanced levels, and "Circuits should always progress from simple to complex, light to strenuous, short to long, and low resistance to high resistance" (PDF p. 316 / printed p. 305, checked against the page image). The progression levers: more stations; more resistance ("especially in strength circuits"); more reps per station; more laps; hybrid exercises at some stations; harder stations replacing easier ones; changing contraction type (concentric, isometric, eccentric); and higher working rate "assessed by heart rate or Rating of Perceived Exertion." Limits: "up to a maximum of about 1 hour for CCT aerobic circuits"; for ICT strength circuits, "increases in resistance necessitate decreases in the number of repetitions and increases in duration of the rest intervals between successive stations." Loads can be set as "a certain percentage of one's 1RM, 6RM or 10RM (Russian system)" or "a certain number of kilograms below one's 1RM, 6RM or 10RM (Bulgarian system)." Testing: "Maximal stress testing ... is not generally advisable for the novice. There should be a pre-testing phase ... It is preferable to start with very light loads ... and to prescribe programmes in terms of adding 5kg, 10kg and so forth to one's starting load. After completion of about three weeks of this pre-testing phase, the trainee may then attempt a 6RM or 10RM. After some three months, it should be safe for the novice to attempt a 1RM, if necessary" (PDF p. 316 / printed p. 305). Aerobic circuit heart-rate targets: "40-50% of maximal recommended heart rate (i.e.: 220 - Age) for beginner circuits," "50-65%" for intermediate and "65-80%" for advanced (PDF p. 317 / printed p. 306, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons for pre-testing are skill and tolerance: the novice must learn "the necessary skills of using the test apparatus and of adapting to the specific nature of the new physical stresses in his life" (PDF p. 316 / printed p. 305). They say "Both systems have their respective merits and deficiencies," that the kilogram (Bulgarian) method "would appear to be more intuitive and generally easier to calculate mentally," and they note both methods share "the disadvantage of being based on testing the trainee with a maximal effort." They add: "individual variations should always be taken into account, and after-exercise condition should be monitored regularly (in terms of tiredness, muscle soreness and other factors discussed in 8.4)" (PDF p. 317 / printed p. 306).

**When to apply** — Group circuits, first-year athletes, and rehab or return groups where a max test would be premature. Eric's baseline: "No sport performs true 1RM testing. Maxes are projected from observation plus the athlete's history." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 61, Explicit, interview Q10). Inference: the authors' "add 5 kg, 10 kg to the starting load" method needs no max at all, which fits that practice better than the percentage system. On heart rate, Eric's baseline: "The anaerobic-threshold heart rate in use is the age-based method" (line 119, Explicit, interview Q20). Inference: the authors' circuit targets use the same 220 - age estimate, but as a percentage of maximum heart rate, not of threshold.
**When NOT to apply** — The three-week and three-month figures are given without a source. The heart-rate bands are percentages of an age-predicted maximum (220 - age), which carries large individual error; the authors call it "a popular method," not a validated one. Inference: 40-50% of age-predicted maximum is a very low intensity for any trained athlete; these bands are written for fitness-centre clients. The Russian and Bulgarian labels are the authors' names for the two methods; no source is given for the attribution.

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 5.20 (verified against the page image, PDF p. 317 / printed p. 306), "A basic multi-level circuit" in which "the total beginner can work twice through the circuit from A to B; after a week or two, he may go 3 times ... and finally ... as many as 6"; intermediates add stations and work "3-6 times through the circuit A to C"; advanced athletes do "3-5 excursions through circuit A to D."
=================== principle--converging-partial-effects-of-strength-training-means.md
confidence: supported
**What it is** — "The principle of converging the partial effects of strength training means is fundamental to the long-term organisation of strength training. It is achieved by ... the gradual convergence of their cumulative training effect to those important specific characteristics which are essential to the functioning of the body in a particular sport" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Early in the sports training process (STP), "the tasks which determine the diversity of the training means are far apart," linked "only by the long-term plan." Specialisation then "is firstly according to ability (but not to the physiological system) and is not related to the motor pattern (see 2.2.3)." "As the STP advances, the training effects of the means begin to converge according to their specificity," until "at the high level of sports mastery the special strength training converges towards the specific character of the motor regime of the given exercise and its specific motor pattern" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295). Fig 5.16 (verified against the page image) plots special fitness against STP time: the key motor ability M and its contributing abilities M1, M2 and M3 start at different, lower levels and curve upward to meet the "Sport A" line at the right of the chart.

**Why it works** — The authors' criterion: "the criterion of successful convergence is the closeness of correspondence of the training effect to the performance characteristics of the given sport." Their account of the late stage: "the effect of the specific training means exceeds the required degree of closeness, while the general training means more strongly reflect the specifics of the special exercise," and "there is a close interrelation between all components which constitute the STP" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295). They give no physiological mechanism.

**When to apply** — Long-term planning: early years can use widely varied means, but each year the means, general ones included, should look more like the sport's motor regime. The authors' role split is useful for planning reviews: "the functional characteristics demanded by the sport determine the requirements of the special strength training, while the level of special fitness determines the progress of the STP as a whole" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295). Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred). Inference: the convergence principle says where an athlete should sit on that spectrum over a career: further toward the specific end each year, with even "general" work chosen to resemble the sport.
**When NOT to apply** — Fig 5.16 is a schematic with no units or data. The principle describes direction over years, not a rule for a single season. The authors say the convergence of general means toward the special exercise happens "As training progresses," so applying it to a beginner would remove the early diversity the same section endorses. Inference: Bondarchuk's correlation tables in this library find that the barbell snatch and half squat transfer to sprinting only within narrow performance bands in most events ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]]), which suggests a general means may stop helping at some levels rather than simply converging; the authors here do not discuss that case.

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 5.16, in which the abilities M1, M2 and M3 that determine the key ability M rise at different rates and converge with M on the profile of sport A by the end of the STP (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295).
